name: Fustat
info: Fustat was the first capital of Egypt under Muslim rule, founded in 641 beside the Roman fortress of Babylon on the east bank of the Nile, and burned in 1168 on the order of its own vizier.

facts.founded: Founded in 641 by the Rashidun general Amr ibn al-As after the fall of Alexandria in September of that year; according to legend a dove's egg in his tent marked the site.
facts.where: On the eastern bank of the Nile, just north of the Roman fortress of Babylon, in what is now the Old Cairo district of Cairo, Egypt.
facts.known: The first capital of Egypt under Muslim rule; the Mosque of Amr, the first mosque in Egypt; a base for Arab expansion in Africa; tall residential buildings; pottery and Islamic art; Maimonides; the burning of 1168
facts.today: Fustat is a suburb within the Old Cairo district of Cairo, where few buildings remain and the buried remains of the old city are still being excavated.

t: Fustat began in 641 as a garrison camp founded by Amr ibn al-As after the capture of Alexandria, and it served as the base for Arab expansion in Africa until Qayrawan was founded in 670.
It grew to about 120,000 people in the 9th century and about 200,000 by 1168, and it was a major centre of Islamic art and ceramics from 975 to 1075.
Shawar, the vizier of the Fatimid caliph, ordered it burned in 1168 to keep it from Amalric of Jerusalem, and the centre of government then moved permanently to nearby Cairo.
dyk: According to al-Maqrizi, the fire that Shawar ordered in 1168, set with 20,000 naphtha pots and 10,000 lighting bombs, burned for 54 days.
ev: Amr ibn al-As founds Fustat after the fall of Alexandria
The Mosque of Amr is built on the site of the commander's tent
The Abbasids take power and move the capital north to al-Askar
Al-Qatta'i is destroyed and the capital returns to Fustat
Gawhar founds Cairo just north of Fustat for the Fatimids
Shawar orders Fustat burned as Amalric's army approaches
Saladin becomes vizier of Egypt and the Ayyubid dynasty begins

sections.origins:
For thousands of years the capital of Egypt moved up and down the Nile with the dynasties, to places such as Thebes and Memphis. After Alexander the Great conquered Egypt around 331 BCE the capital was Alexandria, on the Mediterranean coast, and it remained so for nearly a thousand years. After the army of the caliph Umar captured the region in the 7th century, shortly after the death of Muhammad, a new capital was wanted. When Alexandria fell in September 641, Amr ibn al-As, the commander of the conquering army, founded one on the eastern bank of the river.

According to legend a dove laid an egg in Amr's tent just before he marched against Alexandria. His camp lay just north of the Roman fortress of Babylon. He declared the nest a sign from God and left the tent untouched, and when his troops returned victorious he told them to pitch their tents around his. The city took its name from this, Misr al-Fustat or Fustat Misr, popularly translated as 'city of the tents', though this is not an exact translation. The first mosque in Egypt, the Mosque of Amr, was built in 642 on the site of the commander's tent.
sections.growth:
The early population consisted almost entirely of soldiers and their families, and the city was laid out like a garrison. Amr meant it to be a base from which to conquer North Africa and to launch further campaigns against Byzantium, and it remained the primary base for Arab expansion in Africa until Qayrawan was founded in Tunisia in 670. In the 9th century Fustat was a major city with a population of approximately 120,000.

After the Fatimids founded Cairo to the north the city thrived and grew. In 987 the geographer Ibn Hawkal wrote that Fustat was approximately one third the size of Baghdad, and by 1168 it had a population of 200,000. From 975 to 1075 it was a major production centre for Islamic art and ceramics and one of the wealthiest cities in the world. One report stated that it paid taxes equivalent to US$150,000 a day to the administration of the caliph al-Mu'izz. Excavations have turned up trade goods from as far away as Spain, China and Vietnam.
sections.rulers:
Fustat was the capital of Egypt for approximately 500 years. Its authority was uninterrupted until 750, when the Abbasid dynasty revolted against the Umayyads. Under the Umayyads, who headed the caliphate from 660 to 750, Egypt was a province ruled by governors appointed from other Muslim centres such as Damascus, Medina and Baghdad. The Abbasids, who made Baghdad their centre, moved the Egyptian capital slightly north to their own city of al-Askar, which remained the capital until 868.

When the Tulunid dynasty took control in 868 the capital moved briefly to another northern city, al-Qatta'i. It lasted only until 905, when al-Qatta'i was destroyed and the capital was returned to Fustat. In 969 the Fatimid general Gawhar captured the region and founded Al Qahira (Cairo) just north of Fustat on 8 August, and in 971 the caliph al-Mu'izz moved his court there from al-Mansuriya in Tunisia. Cairo served at first mainly as a royal enclosure for the caliph, his court and his army, while Fustat remained the capital in economic and administrative power. The capital of Egypt is said to have moved to Cairo in 973.
sections.life:
Fustat developed as a series of tribal areas, called khittas, around the central mosque and the administrative buildings. Most of the first settlers came from Yemen, the next largest group came from western Arabia, and there were some Jews and Roman mercenaries. Arabic was generally the primary spoken dialect in Egypt and the language of written communication, though Coptic was still spoken in Fustat in the 8th century.

The city was known for its prosperity, with shaded streets, gardens and markets. It had high-rise residential buildings, some seven storeys tall, which could reportedly accommodate hundreds of people. In the 10th century al-Muqaddasi described them as minarets, and in the early 11th century Nasir Khusraw described some as rising up to 14 storeys, with roof gardens on the top storey and ox-drawn water wheels for irrigation. The Persian traveller Nasir-i-Khusron wrote of the wares in the markets, among them iridescent pottery, crystal and many fruits and flowers, even in winter. Excavations have revealed house and street plans in which a basic unit was a set of rooms built around a central courtyard, entered through an arcade on one side.
sections.crises:
In the mid-12th century the caliph of Egypt was the teenager Athid, whose position was primarily ceremonial. The real power was the vizier Shawar, who for years shifted his alliances between the Crusaders and the forces of Nur al-Din from Syria, keeping each from attacking Egypt. In 1168 King Amalric I of Jerusalem entered Egypt with his army, sacked Bilbeis and slaughtered nearly all of its inhabitants, then camped just south of Fustat and told the caliph to surrender the city or suffer the same fate.

Shawar ordered Fustat burned to keep it out of Amalric's hands. According to the historian al-Maqrizi (1346 to 1442), he ordered the city evacuated and the citizens forced to leave their money and property behind, and he distributed 20,000 naphtha pots and 10,000 lighting bombs through it; the blaze raged for 54 days. Syrian forces then arrived and repelled Amalric, and they went on to conquer Egypt themselves. Shawar was put to death. Under the Mamluks, from the 13th to the 16th century, the area was used as a rubbish dump, though thousands still lived there, mainly potters and rubbish collectors. The layers of garbage built up over hundreds of years and the population gradually fell.
sections.legacy:
After the fire Fustat was no more than a dying suburb, and the centre of government moved permanently to Cairo. Saladin, who became vizier of Egypt on 2 March 1169 and began the Ayyubid dynasty, later tried to unite Cairo and Fustat in one city by enclosing both in massive walls, which was largely unsuccessful. Fustat, al-Askar and al-Qatta'i were all absorbed into the growing city of Cairo.

The physician Maimonides went to Egypt in 1166 and settled in Fustat. He practised in the families of Saladin and his vizier and of Saladin's successors, and wrote his Mishneh Torah there in 1180 and The Guide for the Perplexed. Some of his writings were later found among the manuscript fragments in the geniza of the Ben Ezra Synagogue in Fustat.

Fustat is today a suburb within the Old Cairo district. The Mosque of Amr is still in use, but it has been extensively rebuilt over the centuries and nothing remains of the original structure. The paths of streets are visible, some buildings have been partly reconstructed to waist height, and finds from the site are in Cairo's Museum of Islamic Art. The remains of the original city are believed to lie preserved under centuries of rubbish.

summary: Fustat was founded in 641 by Amr ibn al-As as the first capital of Egypt under Muslim rule. It grew to about 200,000 people and was a centre of ceramics and trade until its vizier Shawar had it burned in 1168. It is now a suburb within Old Cairo.
references: Jere L. Bacharach, Fustat Finds: Beads, Coins, Medical Instruments, Textiles, and Other Artifacts from the Awad Collection (American University in Cairo Press, 2004)
Elinoar Barekeet, Fustat on the Nile: The Jewish Elite in Medieval Egypt (Brill, 1999)
Wladyslaw Kubiak, Al-Fusṭāṭ, its foundation and early urban development (American University in Cairo Press, 1987)
notes: CAPITAL DATES: the article says the capital moved to Cairo in 973, that Cairo was at first only a royal enclosure while Fustat remained the capital in economic and administrative power, and that Fustat was capital for about 500 years. I gave all of this with attribution and did not tidy it; 'is said to have moved' reflects the lead's looser wording. Cairo's founding is 969 (8 August) and the court moved there in 971.

END: the article gives 1168 as the burning, 'no more than a dying suburb' afterwards, yet people still lived there under the Mamluks and it is a suburb today. I set end to 1168 as its end as a capital and city of importance; the editor may prefer null.
POPULATION: peak 'approximately 200,000' in the 12th century, 200,000 by 1168, 120,000 in the 9th century, one third of Baghdad in 987 (Ibn Hawkal). Kept as given.

The article gives the Ibn Hawkal date as 987 and the Nasir Khusraw height of 14 stories against 7 for the buildings generally; both kept with attribution. The tax figure is given in US dollars in the article ('one report stated'); kept hedged.
The article writes 'Nasir Khusraw' and 'Nasir-i-Khusron' for what may be the same man; I kept both spellings as written.

The article gives Alexander's conquest as 'around 331 BC' and the Muslim conquest as AD 641; converted to BCE/CE. Mosque built 642 per the article; the lead and the name section say the first mosque was built in Egypt on the commander's tent site.
The al-Maqrizi quotation is shortened to the evacuation, the naphtha pots and bombs and the 54 days.

Left out: the Mosque of Ibn Tulun, the National Museum of Egyptian Civilisation (2017), the etymology discussion of Misr, the detail of Nur al-Din and the Syrian general Shirkuh, and Mamluk-era detail beyond the dump.

Fatimid dynasty is not named as such in the article's account of Shawar except by 'the reign of the Fatimids was effectively over'; I called Athid 'the caliph of Egypt' and Shawar 'vizier of the Fatimid caliph' in the takeaway, which the article supports by implication only.
The sections run under the guide's lengths in places because the source is short; nothing was padded.
